scenes.headline: Memory-Efficient Large Files
scenes.subtitle: Process data bigger than your RAM
scenes.narration: The core skill here is processing files that are larger than your available memory by streaming them in small pieces rather than loading them all at once.

scenes.headline: The golden rules
items: Never load an entire large file into memory at once
Stream row by row, or in bounded chunks
Keep memory usage constant regardless of file size
scenes.narration: The foundational rule is to never call something like read on a multi-gigabyte file, because that pulls the whole thing into RAM and crashes the process. Instead you stream the data, handling one row or one bounded chunk at a time. Done well, your program's memory footprint stays flat whether the input is one megabyte or one terabyte.

scenes.headline: Load-all vs Stream

columns.title: Load everything
points: Crashes on files larger than RAM

scenes.narration: Loading a whole file is tempting because it is simple and perfectly fine for small inputs. The moment the file exceeds your memory, though, that approach fails outright with a crash. Streaming in chunks costs you a little extra code, but in return your program handles files of any size with a constant, predictable memory profile. For production data engineering, streaming is almost always the right default.

scenes.headline: Line-by-line file streaming
scenes.code:
def count_errors(path):
    errors = 0
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:          # reads one line at a time
            if "ERROR" in line:
                errors += 1
    return errors

print(count_errors("huge.log"))
scenes.narration: Iterating directly over a file object is the simplest streaming pattern in Python. The for loop reads a single line at a time, so only that one line ever lives in memory. This lets you scan a log file of any size while using just a few kilobytes, and the with block guarantees the file is closed even if something goes wrong.

scenes.headline: Chunked reads with pandas
scenes.code:
import pandas as pd

total = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv("huge.csv", chunksize=100_000):
    clean = chunk[chunk["amount"] > 0]
    total += clean["amount"].sum()

print(total)
scenes.narration: When you need pandas' power on a file too big for memory, the chunksize argument turns read_csv into an iterator of DataFrames. Each iteration yields one hundred thousand rows, which you filter and aggregate before moving on. By accumulating only a running total rather than the full data, you get pandas ergonomics on an arbitrarily large file with bounded memory.

scenes.headline: Scaling further
items: Use generators to build lazy processing pipelines
Switch to columnar Parquet for selective, compressed reads
Reach for Dask or Polars when one machine still isn't enough
scenes.narration: You can chain generators together to build lazy pipelines where data flows through many stages one item at a time. Storing data as columnar Parquet lets you read only the columns and row groups you need, cutting both bytes and time. And when a single machine truly cannot keep up, out-of-core engines like Dask or Polars extend these same streaming ideas across chunks and cores automatically.

scenes.text: Stream, don't load — process large files in chunks so memory stays constant no matter how big the input grows.
scenes.narration: The lasting lesson is to stream rather than load, keeping memory constant as inputs grow without bound. Master chunked and lazy processing and file size stops being a limit on what you can compute.
